lines: {target}? Strange quiet can make a place feel too safe. I would stay close enough to hear the bell.
If anyone heads for Mushroom Fields, tell them. Eat only what you know and keep your boat close. I will be at the bell.
Mycelium underfoot is not village dirt. I'll remember that from near the bell.
Mushroom Fields is no small story. Running the wrong way is still running.
I will remember Mushroom Fields as odd land where even the grass changed its mind. I will stay where I can hear the bell.
If I could no longer see the highest mushroom near shore clearly, I would call that a warning.
My feet should vote before I walk through the giant mushrooms by the sea. They usually vote for home.
I would wait for the careful plan at Mushroom Fields. Waiting is easier with bread.
A map of Mushroom Fields would help, especially with a large drawing of the highest mushroom near shore.
Mushroom Fields may be pleasant. It also may have heard me say that and taken it personally.
If my legs started wobbling near the giant mushrooms by the sea, I would listen to them for once.
If soft ocean fog made Mushroom Fields harder to read, I would head back while I could call it my idea.
I can imagine carrying traces of mycelium home from Mushroom Fields.
One torch for seeing and one for finding the first torch again. That is my system.
Seeing the giant mushrooms by the sea would make our village paths seem wonderfully boring. I like boring paths.
I am poor at judging distance, especially when something interesting is at the other end.
I touch things while thinking. Near the giant mushrooms by the sea, I would try thinking with my hands in my pockets.
I remember places by smells I cannot describe. Mushroom Fields sounds likely to become one.
Has anyone counted how many ways losing the shore behind the caps can become a problem? I would stop at one.
There are probably answers at Mushroom Fields. I would settle for returning with the questions.
{target}? Open ground shows you to everything else. I would stay close enough to hear the bell.
If anyone heads for Plains, tell them. Keep moving and watch the horizon. I'll be at the bell.
Grass bends before trouble arrives if you look. I'll remember that from near the bell.
Plains is no small story. Running the wrong way is still running.
I will remember Plains as wide land with nowhere to hide after dark. I will stay where I can hear the bell.
I would bring a map to Plains, though somebody else should hold it the right way up.
For Plains, I would set out early enough to return while the bell still sounded ordinary.
I would try not to make the same mistake twice at Plains. A new mistake is no improvement.
The best part of Plains could be telling the story from my own bed.
I picture Plains and think of the open grass and low paths. Pictures leave out the dangerous walking.
I would warn the group about a zombie beyond the flowers, preferably before my voice became a squeak.
My bag for Plains needs food, torches, and a bedroll. If room remains, I may bring the odd-shaped rock.
At Plains, I would stay close enough to hear the group. I wander better than I return.
I wonder about the smell of grass and packed dirt after an evening shower. I would rather learn from a distance.
A rescue plan should begin at the lone tree near the road, where everyone can find the beginning.
If the plan went wrong, the lone tree near the road should be where it became simple again.
A good memory of Plains weighs less than a full pack and cannot fall on my foot.
At Plains, I would point at suspicious things instead of picking them up. That is progress.
Plains might change quickly under an evening shower. I would keep the route home clear.
I wonder whether bees moving through the flowers would seem louder when everyone stopped talking. I am rarely first to stop.
{target}? Sunny fields can still point toward trouble. I would stay close enough to hear the bell.
If anyone heads for Sunflower Plains, tell them. Enjoy the flowers with a torch ready. I will be at the bell.
Sunflowers face light, not safety. I'll remember that from near the bell.
Sunflower Plains is no small story. Running the wrong way is still running.
I will remember Sunflower Plains as bright fields that still grow dark at night. I will stay where I can hear the bell.
I would warn the group about a bee guarding its nest, preferably before my voice became a squeak.
I would forget one part of Sunflower Plains and remember a completely useless pebble.
I would bring a map to Sunflower Plains, though somebody else should hold it the right way up.
For Sunflower Plains, I would set out early enough to return while the bell still sounded ordinary.
I do not need every shiny thing near the rows of sunflowers across open grass. I have nowhere sensible to put most of them.
I would save torches for the return from Sunflower Plains. The return always gets the leftovers.
I picture Sunflower Plains and think of the rows of sunflowers across open grass. Pictures leave out the dangerous walking.
I would choose a safe place to rest, then ask whether it was safe. The order needs work.
I pack bread for danger and carrots for thinking. I am not sure either works, but they travel well.
I wonder what Sunflower Plains smells like. This is not important, but my nose never asks permission.
Stories never mention bees moving among the sunflowers in enough detail. They leave out useful things like that.
Sunflower Plains would make me curious. It would also make me glad someone else knows when to stop.
Traveling alone gives my ideas too much authority. Sunflower Plains deserves a group decision.
If told not to pull something at Sunflower Plains, I would stand too far away to hear it as a challenge.
I would not let the scenery distract me from a hole hidden behind tall flowers.
